episodes.title: Anthropic's $72M Average Employee, the FAA's 4-Hour Ground Stop, and Starship Caught | EP #313
episodes.summary:
Recorded live with Peter Diamandis hosting while Salim Ismail dials in from Bangkok at 1:00 a.m., this episode of Moonshots (EP #313) joins Dave Blundin and Alex Wissner-Gross for a wide sweep of the week's AI, infrastructure and space news. The pre-show chatter and the opening segment dwell on NVIDIA's leadership turmoil after Jensen Huang's departure. The panel calls it a governance failure and an embarrassment for America's most valuable company. They debate whether activist investors will step in to overhaul the board and whether Jensen could come back the way Steve Jobs did. Alex argues that hyperscalers and frontier labs, partnering with Broadcom or using frontier models to design their own chips, may feel they no longer need NVIDIA's chip design prowess. The group also discusses Google's data advantage and TPUs, and expects a Google plan within roughly 90 to 120 days to shake up frontier-lab infrastructure.

The show then turns to Anthropic's IPO and the wealth boom in San Francisco. Peter cites Bloomberg: at the midpoint of the IPO range the average Anthropic employee would hold about $72 million in shares, with OpenAI insiders near $126 million. Alex laments that frontier labs wait until they are worth roughly $2 trillion to give retail investors exposure, and calls for IPO reform. Peter shares a chart showing time from founding to unicorn status shrinking from 21 years in 2000 to about a year today. The panel notes a talent void at SF universities, since vesting schedules at Anthropic and OpenAI keep employees from leaving, and discusses how that shapes startup hiring and funding.

Next comes infrastructure fragility. The hosts cover a hack that spread through Optimizely (code that tried to hijack crypto payments, skim cards and steal cookies) and the FAA's nationwide ground stop of more than four hours, the longest in 25 years. They argue legacy hardware, old C and C++ code and trusted vendor scripts need modernizing. Cyber offense is now agent-driven and parallel, while defense still has humans in the loop, and they predict a brutal six to eight months before organizations adapt.

The panel celebrates SpaceX's first Starship tower catch and walks through the collapse in cost per kilogram to orbit, previewing an upcoming conversation with Steve Jurvetson. They then take on US-China AI competition, chip restrictions and "Pax Silica," with the view that fabs and hardware, not software, are the only controllable lever. They follow with Elon Musk's rapid AI data-center expansion, the race among top models, and Palmer Luckey's ocean-platform ideas, where skeptics note the sea is corrosive and hard to operate in. The episode closes with audience questions on which business functions move from supervising tasks to supervising outcomes, the purpose of education, AI-driven biology, and application-layer opportunities. The hosts tease a David Sinclair longevity episode.

episodes.title: Anthropic’s $72M Average Employee, SpaceX Catches Starship, and One Hack Hits 178 Sites | LIVE
episodes.summary:
A live Moonshots episode recorded across time zones, with Peter Diamandis hosting alongside Dave Blundin, Alex Wissner-Gross and Salim Ismail, who joins from Bangkok at 1:00 a.m. The cold open covers President Trump landing in China, where Xi Jinping greeted him on the tarmac, and a joke about 1984's three-superpower map. Peter then reports Nvidia's first quarter since Jensen Huang resigned: revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year, data center revenue of about $107 billion, net income of $65 billion, and fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion from interim CEO Colette Kress. The stock still fell about 1.5%. The panel debates the board's succession failure, activist investors, a roughly 30% chance Jensen returns, and what the turmoil means for Google, the frontier labs and chip competitors.

The main business story is Anthropic's IPO. Bloomberg reports that at the midpoint of the IPO range the average Anthropic employee would hold shares worth $72 million, against nearly $126 million for the average OpenAI insider, and that San Francisco absorbs more than a third of global venture capital. Dave calls the concentration of wealth unprecedented, Alex argues it is a travesty that frontier labs wait until they are worth almost $2 trillion to give retail investors direct exposure, and Peter shares a chart showing time-to-unicorn shrinking from 21 years in 2000 to about one year now.

Next comes the week's infrastructure scares: the FAA's nationwide ground stop of more than four hours, which Peter calls the longest in 25 years, with about 12,462 flights cancelled, and a cyberattack in which a flaw in Optimizely's experimentation sign-up flow let attackers inject hostile JavaScript into 178 organizations, including CNN, Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, Salesforce and IKEA. The panel discusses legacy code, offense versus defense asymmetry with AI, and the opportunity in modernizing old systems.

Peter calls Starship Flight 15 the story of the week: Mechazilla caught Ship 42 for the first time after it deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites and flew for about 22.5 hours, with a launch cost-per-kilogram chart and talk of fully reusable spacecraft.

The chips-and-China block covers a possible White House rule requiring US companies to disclose use of Chinese AI models, the fact that the three most used models on OpenRouter in October were Chinese open-weight models, and Alex's view that a "silicon curtain" is descending. Peter says he would rather see a label than a ban. The panel then looks at SpaceX's fast Colossus 2 buildout, OpenAI's GPT 6.2 release and its high self-improvement threshold, and the closure of OpenAI's dedicated robotics team. The episode closes with Palmer Luckey's seasteading render and audience questions on agents supervising outcomes, the future of education, one AI adjusting another's weights, AI biology and virus defense, and a preview of an upcoming David Sinclair longevity episode.

episodes.title: Robotic Deep-Dive: Beating China, the Race Against Tesla, & New Robotics Timeline With Brett Adcock
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis and Dave Blundin visit Figure AI's campus for their annual catch-up with founder and CEO Brett Adcock, about a year after their last visit. Roughly a hundred Figure 03 "visitor bots" greet them outside, able to open doors, climb stairs and ride elevators, and Brett says Figure now has more robots on campus than the company has employees, with well over a thousand on site. Every robot has real-time speech-to-speech, and the team is working on persistent memory so a robot can recall a past conversation.

Brett lays out four stages for the humanoid race: build functional hardware, build an AI recipe, then scale intelligence and scale robots. He says Figure will not ship to homes until the product is Apple-quality, with no teleoperation and no stalling when the robot is unsure, and he warns that rushed launches will fail the way Humane and Rabbit did. Intelligence is the key constraint: Figure 03 can fold laundry, do dishes and unload groceries, but it must do so end to end for a dozen-plus hours a day for years. He points to the early Keurig-cup demo as a turning point because it proved a neural network, rather than C++ code, could drive full upper-body manipulation. He also explains why the team found whole-body teleoperation data matters more than hands and head alone, and why Figure built its Helix model stack from the ground up instead of layering on third-party models.

On competition, Brett says he has not seen much from Tesla in two or three years and names China as the closest competitor, with roughly 150 humanoid companies. He argues Chinese robots optimize for dancing and gymnastics demos, with weak hardware and tiny compute, while Figure targets zero-shot long-horizon work in the home. They discuss the FCC block on Chinese robots, Figure's move away from Chinese parts after tariffs spiked, and the Bay Area as the best place to build robotics.

The conversation also covers a coming Figure 04 he compares to an "iPhone one moment" with a far more human-like hand, a face design debate that rules out googly eyes, financing and leasing of robots, a possible path to a million units a year from one facility, and the case for far more robots than humans by 2040. They touch on chips and memory supply, on whether Figure might go public, and on Hark, Brett's AI-focused effort. They close with regulation, where Brett says the plan is a high-quality, safe product.

episodes.title: Jensen’s Departure, NVIDIA’s Succession Plan, AI Doomer Response, and Demis Talks RSI | #311 (Live)
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis hosts an unscheduled live episode on Friday the 13th, recorded the day after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned, with Emad Mostaque, Alex Wissner-Gross and Salim Ismail. Dave Blundin is absent. Peter opens with the week's number, 13%, how far Nvidia shares fell at the open before closing about 4.3% down. CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO and Harvey Jones the new board chair. The panel works through reporting about an alleged affair with an executive tied to a Singapore company suspected of routing Nvidia chips to China, a Fox News clip framing it as a possible setup, and a Polymarket line giving Jensen roughly a 30% chance of returning as CEO by the end of next year. Alex's theory of the case is that US officials alerted the Financial Times to protect the Pax Silica effort and to ease passage of the Remote Access Security Act after the midterms. Emad finds the board's speed and the timing strange. They weigh a succession problem, since Jensen had about 60 direct reports and the TSMC relationship, and Alex gives a glass-half-full case that the end of circular financing could de-risk the market.

The second block covers AI risk. Paul Christiano, an OpenAI foundation board member, said at the Geoff Hinton lectures that there is a high risk of an AI takeover within three years. Emad, Alex and Salim all push back, with Emad dropping his P(doom) from 50% to 20% and Alex arguing alignment techniques also amplify capabilities. Demis Hassabis's warning about closed-loop recursive self-improvement leads to a debate on whether humans can stay in the loop and whether superintelligence will be alien or familiar.

Next is Anthropic's launch of Claude whiteboard, sheets, data and meetings on November 10, which pushed Microsoft shares down 3.5%. The panel debates whether Office clones are just features and how much Microsoft's roughly $90 billion Office business is at risk. Dario Amodei's claim that cancer, Alzheimer's and heart disease become relics within a decade prompts Alex's "grand bargain" of solving disease in exchange for data centers, and Alex argues virtual cells are the key unlock.

The science segment covers Planet's new Planet AI app for asking questions of a satellite archive, an AI-agent-flagged possible unmapped Mayan site in NASA lidar data, a Fable 5.2 reconstruction of ancient Babylon built in eight hours, and a possible dwarf planet found in Vera Rubin Observatory data using Claude. The episode closes with audience questions on UBI and civil unrest, Nvidia's investment strategy, who gains from exposing the Jensen story, whether Anthropic survives falling token prices, truths beyond human minds, and whether Anthropic keeps a capability gap between internal and public models. An outro song, Terawatt from CJ Trueheart, ends the show.

episodes.title: Jensen’s Spy Probe, Anthropic’s Debut Week, and Elon’s 30M Robot Workforce | #310
episodes.summary:
Peter Diamandis returns to the full five-person panel, with Alex Wissner-Gross, Dave Blundin, Salim Ismail and Emad Mostaque, recorded the week Anthropic launched its IPO roadshow. The cold open covers the alleged espionage probe into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Dave expects the board's investigation to keep surfacing new details, and the panel cites reports of roughly $8 billion of GPUs reaching China through a Singapore-linked network. Alex says it makes the Pax Silica effort look porous. The group predicts security clearances for frontier-model work and a hard push against Chinese open-weight models in regulated industries, and debates whether export controls would turn on nationality rather than ethnicity.

The first main story is Anthropic. The IPO roadshow prices the company at about $1.3 to $1.4 trillion, down from $1.5 trillion and an earlier $2 trillion float, with the listing expected the week before Thanksgiving. Dave thinks pricing it down to give it a pop is smart. The panel then covers Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, which Peter describes as 30% faster than 5.1 and priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Alex highlights robotics, hardware design and operating-system demos and says autonomy time horizons are going nearly vertical. Dave says the model took his spend from $10 to $40 and had designed neural-network accelerator chips in Verilog. Alex's one-sentence prompt produced a cyberpunk first-person shooter with a generated MIDI soundtrack. The panel also discusses a METR-based estimate that time horizons double every two months, and Salim's idea that people can now delegate outcomes rather than tasks.

Dave then challenges the group to have Fable plan how to cure the top 5,000 diseases. An AI-narrated answer argues for approving processes instead of individual drugs, names delivery, diagnosis and cost-and-regulation as the gates, and proposes a kidney or heart delivery prize. Peter shares his own Substack analysis, ranking today's civil unrest ninth and AI seventh among American disruptions. Salim argues institutions cannot absorb "20 Gutenberg moments" at once.

Elon Musk's Baron Investment Conference interview supplies the next segment: Terafab chip production at 30 times current global output, a claimed 100 billion dollar run rate, 20 to 30 million humanoid robots to match US output, a rental model and a possible telco acquisition. Alex says SpaceX is becoming a neo-hyperscaler with Anthropic as its largest customer.

Later stories cover Delaware's draft AI company (AIC) entity, the YC-backed grocery-restocking robot startup Thesius, and NASA's CLPS 2 moon-base contracts, a 10-year, $10 billion ceiling award across eight companies. A Fountain Life health segment says 3.3% of members screened had an undetected cancer. The final story looks at a correlation between more billionaires per capita and less poverty, before a closing Star Trek tribute song.
